### Conclusions and prospects
In conclusion, the PI3K/AKT axis plays a central role in cancer metabolic reprogramming. By precisely regulating key glycolytic metabolic enzymes (e.g., hexokinase, pyruvate kinase, phosphofructokinase, aldolase, lactate dehydrogenase) and related signaling molecules, it profoundly influences the metabolic phenotype of cancer cells. Rate-limiting glycolytic enzymes are subject to direct and indirect modulation by the PI3K/AKT signaling axis. Through alterations in their catalytic activity and expression levels, these enzymes collectively drive hallmark metabolic features of cancer cells, such as the Warburg effect. Rather than acting as a simple switch, this signaling axis executes precise control by modulating the subcellular distribution of key enzymes—such as the mitochondrial association of HK2 and the nuclear translocation of PKM2. These modifications not only drive the classical Warburg effect but also trigger "moonlighting" functions of metabolic enzymes that promote cell survival and immune evasion. Furthermore, the crosstalk between PI3K/AKT and the AMPK sensor ensures that glucose flux is strategically shunted into the PPP and biosynthetic processes to maintain redox balance. Through remodeling glycolytic metabolism, the PI3K/AKT axis further provides cancer cells with sufficient energy supply, essential biosynthetic raw materials, and effective antioxidant protection. Beyond solid tumors, we also emphasize the necessity of considering the unique features of hematological malignancies. Collectively, these molecular mechanism insights demonstrate that targeting the PI3K/AKT-centered metabolic regulatory network is a promising and sophisticated strategy for future precision cancer therapy.

The PI3K/AKT signaling networks in cancer glucose metabolism: mechanisms and therapeutic implications

### Highlights
• Focuses on the PI3K/AKT axis– its core link to cancer metabolic reprogramming (especially the Warburg Effect) and interaction with key glucose metabolic enzymes (HK, LDHA, etc.), as well as their impacts.
• 2. Introduces the non-canonical/moonlighting functions of these glucose metabolic enzymes.
• 3. Provides theoretical basis and potential targets for tumor metabolism research and targeted therapy, along with current research challenges and future directions.

### Introduction
Metabolic reprogramming is a hallmark of cancer, underpinning the rapid proliferation and survival of cancer cells. A cornerstone of this phenomenon is the Warburg effect, where tumor cells predominantly rely on glycolysis for energy even in the presence of oxygen, supports rapid cell proliferation by generating ATP and providing intermediates for biosynthesis processes, such as protein, lipid and nucleotide synthesis [ 1 , 2 ]. This reprogrammed glycolytic phenotype is orchestrated by multiple oncogenic pathways, among which the PI3K/AKT axis represents one of the most potent and commonly activated drivers. Abnormal activation of the PI3K/AKT axis is common in cancer and plays a crucial role in this metabolic shift [ 3 ].
The PI3K/AKT axis regulates a broad array of metabolic pathways, including glycolysis, the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP), oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), de novo lipogenesis, all of which contribute to tumor cell energy demands [ 4 ]. Aberrant activation of this pathway has been implicated in various aspects of cancer biology, such as enhanced glucose uptake, increased glycolytic flux, and altered redox homeostasis. However, the mechanisms by which PI3K/AKT influences key metabolic enzymes remain incompletely understood, particularly with respect to its direct regulation of glycolytic enzymes and the emerging non-canonical functions of these enzymes in tumor.

### The composition and activation mechanisms of the PI3K/AKT pathway
The PI3K/AKT axis is a central signaling pathway critically involved in regulating cell growth, survival, and metabolism. PI3K, a lipid kinase typically comprising a p110 catalytic subunit and p85/p55 regulatory subunits, is frequently dysregulated in human diseases, especially in cancer [ 3 ]. Based on structure and substrate specificity, PI3K can be categorized into three classes. Class I PI3Ks, the primary transducers of extracellular signals, are the most studied [ 3 ]. Activation of this pathway is triggered by various signals, including growth factors (e.g., EGF, IGF), cytokines (e.g., IL-6), hormones, and oncogene activation (e.g., RAS, MYC ) ( Fig. 1 ) [ 4 ]. These ligands bind to cell-surface receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs), such as EGFR, IGF-1R, or cytokine receptors, to initiate downstream signaling cascades. Upon activation, PI3K converts phosphatidylinositol (4,5)-bisphosphate (PIP2) to phosphatidylinositol (3,4,5)-trisphosphate (PIP3). PIP3 recruits AKT to the plasma membrane, where it is partially activated by phosphorylation at Thr308 by phosphoinositide-dependent kinase 1 (PDK1) and fully activated at Ser473 by mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 2 (mTORC2) [ 3 ]. This signaling cascade is negatively regulated by the tumor suppressor PTEN, which dephosphorylates PIP3 back to PIP2. In addition to PTEN-mediated repression, AKT activity is tightly controlled by serine/threonine phosphatase 2A (PP2A). The PP2A regulatory subunit PR130 (encoded by PPP2R3A ) is essential for assembling functional holoenzymes that restrain AKT signaling [ 5 , 6 ]. PP2A directly dephosphorylates AKT at Thr308 and Ser473, thereby suppressing downstream signaling [ 7 ]. Loss of PR130 disrupts PP2A-AKT binding and sustains AKT hyperactivation [ 5 , 6 ]. In hepatocellular carcinoma, aldolase B stabilizes the PP2A-AKT complex to further promote AKT dephosphorylation, underscoring PR130 as a key negative regulator of oncogenic AKT signaling [ 7 ]. ### PI3K/AKT-mediated direct regulation of glycolytic enzymes: metabolic catalysis and emerging non-metabolic roles
In cancer cells, the reprogramming of glucose metabolism is executed by the precise modulation of key glycolytic enzymes. The PI3K/AKT axis sits at the apex of this regulatory network, controlling both the activity and expression of these enzymes to drive the Warburg effect. We illustrate the main steps of glucose metabolism and the regulation of the PI3K/AKT pathway ( Fig. 2 ), and also elaborate on the non-canonical functions of these glycolytic enzymes.
Schematic Illustration of PI3K/AKT-driven Metabolic Reprogramming in Tumor Cells. Activated PI3K/AKT signaling rewires core glucose metabolism by upregulating glycolytic enzymes (HK2, PFK, PKM2, LDHA) to trigger the Warburg effect. Mechanistically, PI3K/AKT-activated PDK1 (3-phosphoinositide-dependent protein kinase 1) suppresses PDH (pyruvate dehydrogenase) activity, restricting pyruvate flux into the TCA (tricarboxylic acid) cycle and subsequent mitochondrial OXPHOS. PI3K/AKT simultaneously promotes PPP-derived NADPH production coupled with GSH (glutathione) to maintain redox homeostasis, and drives de novo lipogenesis via ACLY- and FASN-mediated cascades to fuel cell proliferation, with metabolic crosstalk between de novo lipogenesis and the TCA cycle. ROS (reactive oxygen species) generated by dysfunctional mitochondrial ETC (electron transport chain) I-V reciprocally reactivate upstream PI3K/AKT signaling, forming a positive feedback loop. Small molecule inhibitors targeting PI3K/AKT, key glycolytic enzymes, and OXPHOS are indicated in the diagram. Hexokinase: PI3K/AKT regulation and moonlighting functions
HK is the first rate-limiting enzyme in glycolysis, catalyzing the phosphorylation of glucose to produce glucose-6-phosphate, thereby trapping glucose inside the cell and initiating glycolytic flux. Accumulating evidence confirms a direct correlation between tumor cell growth rate and HK activity [ 18 ]. Among the four HK isoforms (HK1 to HK4), HK2 is of particular importance in cancer. ### Other signaling pathways interacting with the PI3K/AKT pathway
The PI3K/AKT signaling axis acts as a significant regulator of energy metabolism and redox homeostasis, exerting dual effects on the AMPK energy-sensing pathway and multiple glycolysis-associated metabolic pathways. By engaging in reciprocal regulatory crosstalk with AMPK, PI3K/AKT fine-tunes the balance between anabolic and catabolic processes to meet the metabolic demands of cells. Meanwhile, PI3K/AKT modulates PPP, OXPHOS, and de novo lipogenesis—key branches interconnected with glycolysis—to orchestrate metabolic networks that support cell proliferation, survival, and malignant progression.
Crosstalk with AMPK: reciprocal regulation between PI3K/AKT axis and energy sensor
AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) serves as a cellular energy receptor that is activated upon elevation of the AMP/ATP ratio. AMPK, activated under energy shortage and suppressed in its surfeit, inversely regulates glycolysis in accordance with cellular metabolic status. When nutrients are abundant, AMPK attenuates aerobic glycolysis to restrain unnecessary anabolic processes. Conversely, under metabolic stress—particularly glucose scarcity—AMPK shifts its function to promote glycolysis, thereby sustaining ATP production and ensuring short-term cell viability. Activation of the PI3K/AKT axis typically suppresses AMPK activity through multiple mechanisms, including phosphorylating inhibitory sites of AMPK or downregulating upstream kinases of AMPK like LKB1. This inhibition relieves AMPK-mediated suppression of mTORC1 and aerobic glycolysis, allowing tumor cells to maintain a high level of anabolism and support their rapid proliferation and energy demands [ 44 , 45 ]. Consistent with this, studies have found that the deletion of PRKAA1/2 (AMPKα-encoding gene) can lead to an increase in the mRNA expression of ALDOA , LDHA and PDK1 , which all indicate that AMPK negatively regulates the glycolysis process of tumor cells and inhibits tumor growth [ 46 ]. ### Targeted therapeutic strategies for PI3K/AKT-mediated metabolic reprogramming
Metabolic reprogramming is a well-recognized adaptive hallmark of cancer cells, with aberrant glycolysis standing out as one of the most extensively characterized and therapeutically exploitable alterations. Targeting glycolytic enzymes and integrating these agents with other pathway-specific inhibitors or immunotherapies have emerged as promising strategies to overcome tumor cell survival advantages and drug resistance.

### Therapeutic targeting of metabolic enzymes in the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway
Aberrant glycolytic metabolism, a hallmark of cancer, offers a fertile ground for therapeutic intervention. By targeting key enzymes that drive this metabolic reprogramming, it is possible to disrupt the energy supply and biosynthetic pathways essential for cancer growth and survival. ### Conclusions and prospects
In conclusion, the PI3K/AKT axis plays a central role in cancer metabolic reprogramming. By precisely regulating key glycolytic metabolic enzymes (e.g., hexokinase, pyruvate kinase, phosphofructokinase, aldolase, lactate dehydrogenase) and related signaling molecules, it profoundly influences the metabolic phenotype of cancer cells. Rate-limiting glycolytic enzymes are subject to direct and indirect modulation by the PI3K/AKT signaling axis. Through alterations in their catalytic activity and expression levels, these enzymes collectively drive hallmark metabolic features of cancer cells, such as the Warburg effect. Rather than acting as a simple switch, this signaling axis executes precise control by modulating the subcellular distribution of key enzymes—such as the mitochondrial association of HK2 and the nuclear translocation of PKM2. These modifications not only drive the classical Warburg effect but also trigger "moonlighting" functions of metabolic enzymes that promote cell survival and immune evasion. Furthermore, the crosstalk between PI3K/AKT and the AMPK sensor ensures that glucose flux is strategically shunted into the PPP and biosynthetic processes to maintain redox balance. Through remodeling glycolytic metabolism, the PI3K/AKT axis further provides cancer cells with sufficient energy supply, essential biosynthetic raw materials, and effective antioxidant protection. Beyond solid tumors, we also emphasize the necessity of considering the unique features of hematological malignancies. Collectively, these molecular mechanism insights demonstrate that targeting the PI3K/AKT-centered metabolic regulatory network is a promising and sophisticated strategy for future precision cancer therapy.

### Highlights
• Focuses on the PI3K/AKT axis– its core link to cancer metabolic reprogramming (especially the Warburg Effect) and interaction with key glucose metabolic enzymes (HK, LDHA, etc.), as well as their impacts.
• 2. Introduces the non-canonical/moonlighting functions of these glucose metabolic enzymes.
• 3. Provides theoretical basis and potential targets for tumor metabolism research and targeted therapy, along with current research challenges and future directions.

### Introduction
Metabolic reprogramming is a hallmark of cancer, underpinning the rapid proliferation and survival of cancer cells. A cornerstone of this phenomenon is the Warburg effect, where tumor cells predominantly rely on glycolysis for energy even in the presence of oxygen, supports rapid cell proliferation by generating ATP and providing intermediates for biosynthesis processes, such as protein, lipid and nucleotide synthesis [ 1 , 2 ]. This reprogrammed glycolytic phenotype is orchestrated by multiple oncogenic pathways, among which the PI3K/AKT axis represents one of the most potent and commonly activated drivers. Abnormal activation of the PI3K/AKT axis is common in cancer and plays a crucial role in this metabolic shift [ 3 ].
The PI3K/AKT axis regulates a broad array of metabolic pathways, including glycolysis, the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP), oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), de novo lipogenesis, all of which contribute to tumor cell energy demands [ 4 ]. Aberrant activation of this pathway has been implicated in various aspects of cancer biology, such as enhanced glucose uptake, increased glycolytic flux, and altered redox homeostasis. However, the mechanisms by which PI3K/AKT influences key metabolic enzymes remain incompletely understood, particularly with respect to its direct regulation of glycolytic enzymes and the emerging non-canonical functions of these enzymes in tumor.

### The composition and activation mechanisms of the PI3K/AKT pathway
The PI3K/AKT axis is a central signaling pathway critically involved in regulating cell growth, survival, and metabolism. PI3K, a lipid kinase typically comprising a p110 catalytic subunit and p85/p55 regulatory subunits, is frequently dysregulated in human diseases, especially in cancer [ 3 ]. Based on structure and substrate specificity, PI3K can be categorized into three classes. Class I PI3Ks, the primary transducers of extracellular signals, are the most studied [ 3 ]. Activation of this pathway is triggered by various signals, including growth factors (e.g., EGF, IGF), cytokines (e.g., IL-6), hormones, and oncogene activation (e.g., RAS, MYC ) ( Fig. 1 ) [ 4 ]. These ligands bind to cell-surface receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs), such as EGFR, IGF-1R, or cytokine receptors, to initiate downstream signaling cascades. Upon activation, PI3K converts phosphatidylinositol (4,5)-bisphosphate (PIP2) to phosphatidylinositol (3,4,5)-trisphosphate (PIP3). PIP3 recruits AKT to the plasma membrane, where it is partially activated by phosphorylation at Thr308 by phosphoinositide-dependent kinase 1 (PDK1) and fully activated at Ser473 by mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 2 (mTORC2) [ 3 ]. This signaling cascade is negatively regulated by the tumor suppressor PTEN, which dephosphorylates PIP3 back to PIP2. In addition to PTEN-mediated repression, AKT activity is tightly controlled by serine/threonine phosphatase 2A (PP2A). The PP2A regulatory subunit PR130 (encoded by PPP2R3A ) is essential for assembling functional holoenzymes that restrain AKT signaling [ 5 , 6 ]. PP2A directly dephosphorylates AKT at Thr308 and Ser473, thereby suppressing downstream signaling [ 7 ]. Loss of PR130 disrupts PP2A-AKT binding and sustains AKT hyperactivation [ 5 , 6 ]. In hepatocellular carcinoma, aldolase B stabilizes the PP2A-AKT complex to further promote AKT dephosphorylation, underscoring PR130 as a key negative regulator of oncogenic AKT signaling [ 7 ]. ### PI3K/AKT-mediated direct regulation of glycolytic enzymes: metabolic catalysis and emerging non-metabolic roles
In cancer cells, the reprogramming of glucose metabolism is executed by the precise modulation of key glycolytic enzymes. The PI3K/AKT axis sits at the apex of this regulatory network, controlling both the activity and expression of these enzymes to drive the Warburg effect. We illustrate the main steps of glucose metabolism and the regulation of the PI3K/AKT pathway ( Fig. 2 ), and also elaborate on the non-canonical functions of these glycolytic enzymes.
Schematic Illustration of PI3K/AKT-driven Metabolic Reprogramming in Tumor Cells. Activated PI3K/AKT signaling rewires core glucose metabolism by upregulating glycolytic enzymes (HK2, PFK, PKM2, LDHA) to trigger the Warburg effect. Mechanistically, PI3K/AKT-activated PDK1 (3-phosphoinositide-dependent protein kinase 1) suppresses PDH (pyruvate dehydrogenase) activity, restricting pyruvate flux into the TCA (tricarboxylic acid) cycle and subsequent mitochondrial OXPHOS. PI3K/AKT simultaneously promotes PPP-derived NADPH production coupled with GSH (glutathione) to maintain redox homeostasis, and drives de novo lipogenesis via ACLY- and FASN-mediated cascades to fuel cell proliferation, with metabolic crosstalk between de novo lipogenesis and the TCA cycle. ROS (reactive oxygen species) generated by dysfunctional mitochondrial ETC (electron transport chain) I-V reciprocally reactivate upstream PI3K/AKT signaling, forming a positive feedback loop. Small molecule inhibitors targeting PI3K/AKT, key glycolytic enzymes, and OXPHOS are indicated in the diagram. Hexokinase: PI3K/AKT regulation and moonlighting functions
HK is the first rate-limiting enzyme in glycolysis, catalyzing the phosphorylation of glucose to produce glucose-6-phosphate, thereby trapping glucose inside the cell and initiating glycolytic flux. Accumulating evidence confirms a direct correlation between tumor cell growth rate and HK activity [ 18 ]. Among the four HK isoforms (HK1 to HK4), HK2 is of particular importance in cancer. ### Other signaling pathways interacting with the PI3K/AKT pathway
The PI3K/AKT signaling axis acts as a significant regulator of energy metabolism and redox homeostasis, exerting dual effects on the AMPK energy-sensing pathway and multiple glycolysis-associated metabolic pathways. By engaging in reciprocal regulatory crosstalk with AMPK, PI3K/AKT fine-tunes the balance between anabolic and catabolic processes to meet the metabolic demands of cells. Meanwhile, PI3K/AKT modulates PPP, OXPHOS, and de novo lipogenesis—key branches interconnected with glycolysis—to orchestrate metabolic networks that support cell proliferation, survival, and malignant progression.
Crosstalk with AMPK: reciprocal regulation between PI3K/AKT axis and energy sensor
AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) serves as a cellular energy receptor that is activated upon elevation of the AMP/ATP ratio. AMPK, activated under energy shortage and suppressed in its surfeit, inversely regulates glycolysis in accordance with cellular metabolic status. When nutrients are abundant, AMPK attenuates aerobic glycolysis to restrain unnecessary anabolic processes. Conversely, under metabolic stress—particularly glucose scarcity—AMPK shifts its function to promote glycolysis, thereby sustaining ATP production and ensuring short-term cell viability. Activation of the PI3K/AKT axis typically suppresses AMPK activity through multiple mechanisms, including phosphorylating inhibitory sites of AMPK or downregulating upstream kinases of AMPK like LKB1. This inhibition relieves AMPK-mediated suppression of mTORC1 and aerobic glycolysis, allowing tumor cells to maintain a high level of anabolism and support their rapid proliferation and energy demands [ 44 , 45 ]. Consistent with this, studies have found that the deletion of PRKAA1/2 (AMPKα-encoding gene) can lead to an increase in the mRNA expression of ALDOA , LDHA and PDK1 , which all indicate that AMPK negatively regulates the glycolysis process of tumor cells and inhibits tumor growth [ 46 ]. ### Targeted therapeutic strategies for PI3K/AKT-mediated metabolic reprogramming
Metabolic reprogramming is a well-recognized adaptive hallmark of cancer cells, with aberrant glycolysis standing out as one of the most extensively characterized and therapeutically exploitable alterations. Targeting glycolytic enzymes and integrating these agents with other pathway-specific inhibitors or immunotherapies have emerged as promising strategies to overcome tumor cell survival advantages and drug resistance.

### Therapeutic targeting of metabolic enzymes in the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway
Aberrant glycolytic metabolism, a hallmark of cancer, offers a fertile ground for therapeutic intervention. By targeting key enzymes that drive this metabolic reprogramming, it is possible to disrupt the energy supply and biosynthetic pathways essential for cancer growth and survival. ### Conclusions and prospects
In conclusion, the PI3K/AKT axis plays a central role in cancer metabolic reprogramming. By precisely regulating key glycolytic metabolic enzymes (e.g., hexokinase, pyruvate kinase, phosphofructokinase, aldolase, lactate dehydrogenase) and related signaling molecules, it profoundly influences the metabolic phenotype of cancer cells. Rate-limiting glycolytic enzymes are subject to direct and indirect modulation by the PI3K/AKT signaling axis. Through alterations in their catalytic activity and expression levels, these enzymes collectively drive hallmark metabolic features of cancer cells, such as the Warburg effect. Rather than acting as a simple switch, this signaling axis executes precise control by modulating the subcellular distribution of key enzymes—such as the mitochondrial association of HK2 and the nuclear translocation of PKM2. These modifications not only drive the classical Warburg effect but also trigger "moonlighting" functions of metabolic enzymes that promote cell survival and immune evasion. Furthermore, the crosstalk between PI3K/AKT and the AMPK sensor ensures that glucose flux is strategically shunted into the PPP and biosynthetic processes to maintain redox balance. Through remodeling glycolytic metabolism, the PI3K/AKT axis further provides cancer cells with sufficient energy supply, essential biosynthetic raw materials, and effective antioxidant protection. Beyond solid tumors, we also emphasize the necessity of considering the unique features of hematological malignancies. Collectively, these molecular mechanism insights demonstrate that targeting the PI3K/AKT-centered metabolic regulatory network is a promising and sophisticated strategy for future precision cancer therapy.

### Highlights
• Focuses on the PI3K/AKT axis– its core link to cancer metabolic reprogramming (especially the Warburg Effect) and interaction with key glucose metabolic enzymes (HK, LDHA, etc.), as well as their impacts.
• 2. Introduces the non-canonical/moonlighting functions of these glucose metabolic enzymes.
• 3. Provides theoretical basis and potential targets for tumor metabolism research and targeted therapy, along with current research challenges and future directions.

### Introduction
Metabolic reprogramming is a hallmark of cancer, underpinning the rapid proliferation and survival of cancer cells. A cornerstone of this phenomenon is the Warburg effect, where tumor cells predominantly rely on glycolysis for energy even in the presence of oxygen, supports rapid cell proliferation by generating ATP and providing intermediates for biosynthesis processes, such as protein, lipid and nucleotide synthesis [ 1 , 2 ]. This reprogrammed glycolytic phenotype is orchestrated by multiple oncogenic pathways, among which the PI3K/AKT axis represents one of the most potent and commonly activated drivers. Abnormal activation of the PI3K/AKT axis is common in cancer and plays a crucial role in this metabolic shift [ 3 ].
The PI3K/AKT axis regulates a broad array of metabolic pathways, including glycolysis, the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP), oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), de novo lipogenesis, all of which contribute to tumor cell energy demands [ 4 ]. Aberrant activation of this pathway has been implicated in various aspects of cancer biology, such as enhanced glucose uptake, increased glycolytic flux, and altered redox homeostasis. However, the mechanisms by which PI3K/AKT influences key metabolic enzymes remain incompletely understood, particularly with respect to its direct regulation of glycolytic enzymes and the emerging non-canonical functions of these enzymes in tumor.

### The composition and activation mechanisms of the PI3K/AKT pathway
The PI3K/AKT axis is a central signaling pathway critically involved in regulating cell growth, survival, and metabolism. PI3K, a lipid kinase typically comprising a p110 catalytic subunit and p85/p55 regulatory subunits, is frequently dysregulated in human diseases, especially in cancer [ 3 ]. Based on structure and substrate specificity, PI3K can be categorized into three classes. Class I PI3Ks, the primary transducers of extracellular signals, are the most studied [ 3 ]. Activation of this pathway is triggered by various signals, including growth factors (e.g., EGF, IGF), cytokines (e.g., IL-6), hormones, and oncogene activation (e.g., RAS, MYC ) ( Fig. 1 ) [ 4 ]. These ligands bind to cell-surface receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs), such as EGFR, IGF-1R, or cytokine receptors, to initiate downstream signaling cascades. Upon activation, PI3K converts phosphatidylinositol (4,5)-bisphosphate (PIP2) to phosphatidylinositol (3,4,5)-trisphosphate (PIP3). PIP3 recruits AKT to the plasma membrane, where it is partially activated by phosphorylation at Thr308 by phosphoinositide-dependent kinase 1 (PDK1) and fully activated at Ser473 by mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 2 (mTORC2) [ 3 ]. This signaling cascade is negatively regulated by the tumor suppressor PTEN, which dephosphorylates PIP3 back to PIP2. In addition to PTEN-mediated repression, AKT activity is tightly controlled by serine/threonine phosphatase 2A (PP2A). The PP2A regulatory subunit PR130 (encoded by PPP2R3A ) is essential for assembling functional holoenzymes that restrain AKT signaling [ 5 , 6 ]. PP2A directly dephosphorylates AKT at Thr308 and Ser473, thereby suppressing downstream signaling [ 7 ]. Loss of PR130 disrupts PP2A-AKT binding and sustains AKT hyperactivation [ 5 , 6 ]. In hepatocellular carcinoma, aldolase B stabilizes the PP2A-AKT complex to further promote AKT dephosphorylation, underscoring PR130 as a key negative regulator of oncogenic AKT signaling [ 7 ]. ### PI3K/AKT-mediated direct regulation of glycolytic enzymes: metabolic catalysis and emerging non-metabolic roles
In cancer cells, the reprogramming of glucose metabolism is executed by the precise modulation of key glycolytic enzymes. The PI3K/AKT axis sits at the apex of this regulatory network, controlling both the activity and expression of these enzymes to drive the Warburg effect. We illustrate the main steps of glucose metabolism and the regulation of the PI3K/AKT pathway ( Fig. 2 ), and also elaborate on the non-canonical functions of these glycolytic enzymes.
Schematic Illustration of PI3K/AKT-driven Metabolic Reprogramming in Tumor Cells. Activated PI3K/AKT signaling rewires core glucose metabolism by upregulating glycolytic enzymes (HK2, PFK, PKM2, LDHA) to trigger the Warburg effect. Mechanistically, PI3K/AKT-activated PDK1 (3-phosphoinositide-dependent protein kinase 1) suppresses PDH (pyruvate dehydrogenase) activity, restricting pyruvate flux into the TCA (tricarboxylic acid) cycle and subsequent mitochondrial OXPHOS. PI3K/AKT simultaneously promotes PPP-derived NADPH production coupled with GSH (glutathione) to maintain redox homeostasis, and drives de novo lipogenesis via ACLY- and FASN-mediated cascades to fuel cell proliferation, with metabolic crosstalk between de novo lipogenesis and the TCA cycle. ROS (reactive oxygen species) generated by dysfunctional mitochondrial ETC (electron transport chain) I-V reciprocally reactivate upstream PI3K/AKT signaling, forming a positive feedback loop. Small molecule inhibitors targeting PI3K/AKT, key glycolytic enzymes, and OXPHOS are indicated in the diagram. Hexokinase: PI3K/AKT regulation and moonlighting functions
HK is the first rate-limiting enzyme in glycolysis, catalyzing the phosphorylation of glucose to produce glucose-6-phosphate, thereby trapping glucose inside the cell and initiating glycolytic flux. Accumulating evidence confirms a direct correlation between tumor cell growth rate and HK activity [ 18 ]. Among the four HK isoforms (HK1 to HK4), HK2 is of particular importance in cancer. ### Other signaling pathways interacting with the PI3K/AKT pathway
The PI3K/AKT signaling axis acts as a significant regulator of energy metabolism and redox homeostasis, exerting dual effects on the AMPK energy-sensing pathway and multiple glycolysis-associated metabolic pathways. By engaging in reciprocal regulatory crosstalk with AMPK, PI3K/AKT fine-tunes the balance between anabolic and catabolic processes to meet the metabolic demands of cells. Meanwhile, PI3K/AKT modulates PPP, OXPHOS, and de novo lipogenesis—key branches interconnected with glycolysis—to orchestrate metabolic networks that support cell proliferation, survival, and malignant progression.
Crosstalk with AMPK: reciprocal regulation between PI3K/AKT axis and energy sensor
AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) serves as a cellular energy receptor that is activated upon elevation of the AMP/ATP ratio. AMPK, activated under energy shortage and suppressed in its surfeit, inversely regulates glycolysis in accordance with cellular metabolic status. When nutrients are abundant, AMPK attenuates aerobic glycolysis to restrain unnecessary anabolic processes. Conversely, under metabolic stress—particularly glucose scarcity—AMPK shifts its function to promote glycolysis, thereby sustaining ATP production and ensuring short-term cell viability. Activation of the PI3K/AKT axis typically suppresses AMPK activity through multiple mechanisms, including phosphorylating inhibitory sites of AMPK or downregulating upstream kinases of AMPK like LKB1. This inhibition relieves AMPK-mediated suppression of mTORC1 and aerobic glycolysis, allowing tumor cells to maintain a high level of anabolism and support their rapid proliferation and energy demands [ 44 , 45 ]. Consistent with this, studies have found that the deletion of PRKAA1/2 (AMPKα-encoding gene) can lead to an increase in the mRNA expression of ALDOA , LDHA and PDK1 , which all indicate that AMPK negatively regulates the glycolysis process of tumor cells and inhibits tumor growth [ 46 ]. ### Targeted therapeutic strategies for PI3K/AKT-mediated metabolic reprogramming
Metabolic reprogramming is a well-recognized adaptive hallmark of cancer cells, with aberrant glycolysis standing out as one of the most extensively characterized and therapeutically exploitable alterations. Targeting glycolytic enzymes and integrating these agents with other pathway-specific inhibitors or immunotherapies have emerged as promising strategies to overcome tumor cell survival advantages and drug resistance.

### Therapeutic targeting of metabolic enzymes in the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway
Aberrant glycolytic metabolism, a hallmark of cancer, offers a fertile ground for therapeutic intervention. By targeting key enzymes that drive this metabolic reprogramming, it is possible to disrupt the energy supply and biosynthetic pathways essential for cancer growth and survival. ### Conclusions and prospects
In conclusion, the PI3K/AKT axis plays a central role in cancer metabolic reprogramming. By precisely regulating key glycolytic metabolic enzymes (e.g., hexokinase, pyruvate kinase, phosphofructokinase, aldolase, lactate dehydrogenase) and related signaling molecules, it profoundly influences the metabolic phenotype of cancer cells. Rate-limiting glycolytic enzymes are subject to direct and indirect modulation by the PI3K/AKT signaling axis. Through alterations in their catalytic activity and expression levels, these enzymes collectively drive hallmark metabolic features of cancer cells, such as the Warburg effect. Rather than acting as a simple switch, this signaling axis executes precise control by modulating the subcellular distribution of key enzymes—such as the mitochondrial association of HK2 and the nuclear translocation of PKM2. These modifications not only drive the classical Warburg effect but also trigger "moonlighting" functions of metabolic enzymes that promote cell survival and immune evasion. Furthermore, the crosstalk between PI3K/AKT and the AMPK sensor ensures that glucose flux is strategically shunted into the PPP and biosynthetic processes to maintain redox balance. Through remodeling glycolytic metabolism, the PI3K/AKT axis further provides cancer cells with sufficient energy supply, essential biosynthetic raw materials, and effective antioxidant protection. Beyond solid tumors, we also emphasize the necessity of considering the unique features of hematological malignancies. Collectively, these molecular mechanism insights demonstrate that targeting the PI3K/AKT-centered metabolic regulatory network is a promising and sophisticated strategy for future precision cancer therapy.

### Introduction
Metabolic reprogramming is a hallmark of cancer, underpinning the rapid proliferation and survival of cancer cells. A cornerstone of this phenomenon is the Warburg effect, where tumor cells predominantly rely on glycolysis for energy even in the presence of oxygen, supports rapid cell proliferation by generating ATP and providing intermediates for biosynthesis processes, such as protein, lipid and nucleotide synthesis [ 1 , 2 ]. This reprogrammed glycolytic phenotype is orchestrated by multiple oncogenic pathways, among which the PI3K/AKT axis represents one of the most potent and commonly activated drivers. Abnormal activation of the PI3K/AKT axis is common in cancer and plays a crucial role in this metabolic shift [ 3 ].
The PI3K/AKT axis regulates a broad array of metabolic pathways, including glycolysis, the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP), oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), de novo lipogenesis, all of which contribute to tumor cell energy demands [ 4 ]. Aberrant activation of this pathway has been implicated in various aspects of cancer biology, such as enhanced glucose uptake, increased glycolytic flux, and altered redox homeostasis. However, the mechanisms by which PI3K/AKT influences key metabolic enzymes remain incompletely understood, particularly with respect to its direct regulation of glycolytic enzymes and the emerging non-canonical functions of these enzymes in tumor.

### The composition and activation mechanisms of the PI3K/AKT pathway

Based on structure and substrate specificity, PI3K can be categorized into three classes. Class I PI3Ks, the primary transducers of extracellular signals, are the most studied [ 3 ]. Activation of this pathway is triggered by various signals, including growth factors (e.g., EGF, IGF), cytokines (e.g., IL-6), hormones, and oncogene activation (e.g., RAS, MYC ) ( Fig. 1 ) [ 4 ]. These ligands bind to cell-surface receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs), such as EGFR, IGF-1R, or cytokine receptors, to initiate downstream signaling cascades. Upon activation, PI3K converts phosphatidylinositol (4,5)-bisphosphate (PIP2) to phosphatidylinositol (3,4,5)-trisphosphate (PIP3). PIP3 recruits AKT to the plasma membrane, where it is partially activated by phosphorylation at Thr308 by phosphoinositide-dependent kinase 1 (PDK1) and fully activated at Ser473 by mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 2 (mTORC2) [ 3 ]. This signaling cascade is negatively regulated by the tumor suppressor PTEN, which dephosphorylates PIP3 back to PIP2. In addition to PTEN-mediated repression, AKT activity is tightly controlled by serine/threonine phosphatase 2A (PP2A). The PP2A regulatory subunit PR130 (encoded by PPP2R3A ) is essential for assembling functional holoenzymes that restrain AKT signaling [ 5 , 6 ]. PP2A directly dephosphorylates AKT at Thr308 and Ser473, thereby suppressing downstream signaling [ 7 ]. Loss of PR130 disrupts PP2A-AKT binding and sustains AKT hyperactivation [ 5 , 6 ]. In hepatocellular carcinoma, aldolase B stabilizes the PP2A-AKT complex to further promote AKT dephosphorylation, underscoring PR130 as a key negative regulator of oncogenic AKT signaling [ 7 ]. ### PI3K/AKT-mediated direct regulation of glycolytic enzymes: metabolic catalysis and emerging non-metabolic roles
In cancer cells, the reprogramming of glucose metabolism is executed by the precise modulation of key glycolytic enzymes. The PI3K/AKT axis sits at the apex of this regulatory network, controlling both the activity and expression of these enzymes to drive the Warburg effect. We illustrate the main steps of glucose metabolism and the regulation of the PI3K/AKT pathway ( Fig. 2 ), and also elaborate on the non-canonical functions of these glycolytic enzymes.
Schematic Illustration of PI3K/AKT-driven Metabolic Reprogramming in Tumor Cells. Activated PI3K/AKT signaling rewires core glucose metabolism by upregulating glycolytic enzymes (HK2, PFK, PKM2, LDHA) to trigger the Warburg effect. Mechanistically, PI3K/AKT-activated PDK1 (3-phosphoinositide-dependent protein kinase 1) suppresses PDH (pyruvate dehydrogenase) activity, restricting pyruvate flux into the TCA (tricarboxylic acid) cycle and subsequent mitochondrial OXPHOS. PI3K/AKT simultaneously promotes PPP-derived NADPH production coupled with GSH (glutathione) to maintain redox homeostasis, and drives de novo lipogenesis via ACLY- and FASN-mediated cascades to fuel cell proliferation, with metabolic crosstalk between de novo lipogenesis and the TCA cycle. ROS (reactive oxygen species) generated by dysfunctional mitochondrial ETC (electron transport chain) I-V reciprocally reactivate upstream PI3K/AKT signaling, forming a positive feedback loop. Small molecule inhibitors targeting PI3K/AKT, key glycolytic enzymes, and OXPHOS are indicated in the diagram. Hexokinase: PI3K/AKT regulation and moonlighting functions
HK is the first rate-limiting enzyme in glycolysis, catalyzing the phosphorylation of glucose to produce glucose-6-phosphate, thereby trapping glucose inside the cell and initiating glycolytic flux. Accumulating evidence confirms a direct correlation between tumor cell growth rate and HK activity [ 18 ]. Among the four HK isoforms (HK1 to HK4), HK2 is of particular importance in cancer. ### Other signaling pathways interacting with the PI3K/AKT pathway
The PI3K/AKT signaling axis acts as a significant regulator of energy metabolism and redox homeostasis, exerting dual effects on the AMPK energy-sensing pathway and multiple glycolysis-associated metabolic pathways. By engaging in reciprocal regulatory crosstalk with AMPK, PI3K/AKT fine-tunes the balance between anabolic and catabolic processes to meet the metabolic demands of cells. Meanwhile, PI3K/AKT modulates PPP, OXPHOS, and de novo lipogenesis—key branches interconnected with glycolysis—to orchestrate metabolic networks that support cell proliferation, survival, and malignant progression.
Crosstalk with AMPK: reciprocal regulation between PI3K/AKT axis and energy sensor
AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) serves as a cellular energy receptor that is activated upon elevation of the AMP/ATP ratio. AMPK, activated under energy shortage and suppressed in its surfeit, inversely regulates glycolysis in accordance with cellular metabolic status. When nutrients are abundant, AMPK attenuates aerobic glycolysis to restrain unnecessary anabolic processes. Conversely, under metabolic stress—particularly glucose scarcity—AMPK shifts its function to promote glycolysis, thereby sustaining ATP production and ensuring short-term cell viability. Activation of the PI3K/AKT axis typically suppresses AMPK activity through multiple mechanisms, including phosphorylating inhibitory sites of AMPK or downregulating upstream kinases of AMPK like LKB1. This inhibition relieves AMPK-mediated suppression of mTORC1 and aerobic glycolysis, allowing tumor cells to maintain a high level of anabolism and support their rapid proliferation and energy demands [ 44 , 45 ]. Consistent with this, studies have found that the deletion of PRKAA1/2 (AMPKα-encoding gene) can lead to an increase in the mRNA expression of ALDOA , LDHA and PDK1 , which all indicate that AMPK negatively regulates the glycolysis process of tumor cells and inhibits tumor growth [ 46 ]. ### Targeted therapeutic strategies for PI3K/AKT-mediated metabolic reprogramming
Metabolic reprogramming is a well-recognized adaptive hallmark of cancer cells, with aberrant glycolysis standing out as one of the most extensively characterized and therapeutically exploitable alterations. Targeting glycolytic enzymes and integrating these agents with other pathway-specific inhibitors or immunotherapies have emerged as promising strategies to overcome tumor cell survival advantages and drug resistance.

### Therapeutic targeting of metabolic enzymes in the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway
Aberrant glycolytic metabolism, a hallmark of cancer, offers a fertile ground for therapeutic intervention. By targeting key enzymes that drive this metabolic reprogramming, it is possible to disrupt the energy supply and biosynthetic pathways essential for cancer growth and survival. ### Conclusions and prospects
In conclusion, the PI3K/AKT axis plays a central role in cancer metabolic reprogramming. By precisely regulating key glycolytic metabolic enzymes (e.g., hexokinase, pyruvate kinase, phosphofructokinase, aldolase, lactate dehydrogenase) and related signaling molecules, it profoundly influences the metabolic phenotype of cancer cells. Rate-limiting glycolytic enzymes are subject to direct and indirect modulation by the PI3K/AKT signaling axis. Through alterations in their catalytic activity and expression levels, these enzymes collectively drive hallmark metabolic features of cancer cells, such as the Warburg effect. Rather than acting as a simple switch, this signaling axis executes precise control by modulating the subcellular distribution of key enzymes—such as the mitochondrial association of HK2 and the nuclear translocation of PKM2. These modifications not only drive the classical Warburg effect but also trigger "moonlighting" functions of metabolic enzymes that promote cell survival and immune evasion. Furthermore, the crosstalk between PI3K/AKT and the AMPK sensor ensures that glucose flux is strategically shunted into the PPP and biosynthetic processes to maintain redox balance. Through remodeling glycolytic metabolism, the PI3K/AKT axis further provides cancer cells with sufficient energy supply, essential biosynthetic raw materials, and effective antioxidant protection. Beyond solid tumors, we also emphasize the necessity of considering the unique features of hematological malignancies. Collectively, these molecular mechanism insights demonstrate that targeting the PI3K/AKT-centered metabolic regulatory network is a promising and sophisticated strategy for future precision cancer therapy.

### Highlights
• Focuses on the PI3K/AKT axis– its core link to cancer metabolic reprogramming (especially the Warburg Effect) and interaction with key glucose metabolic enzymes (HK, LDHA, etc.), as well as their impacts.
• 2. Introduces the non-canonical/moonlighting functions of these glucose metabolic enzymes.
• 3. Provides theoretical basis and potential targets for tumor metabolism research and targeted therapy, along with current research challenges and future directions.

### Introduction
Metabolic reprogramming is a hallmark of cancer, underpinning the rapid proliferation and survival of cancer cells. A cornerstone of this phenomenon is the Warburg effect, where tumor cells predominantly rely on glycolysis for energy even in the presence of oxygen, supports rapid cell proliferation by generating ATP and providing intermediates for biosynthesis processes, such as protein, lipid and nucleotide synthesis [ 1 , 2 ]. This reprogrammed glycolytic phenotype is orchestrated by multiple oncogenic pathways, among which the PI3K/AKT axis represents one of the most potent and commonly activated drivers. Abnormal activation of the PI3K/AKT axis is common in cancer and plays a crucial role in this metabolic shift [ 3 ].
The PI3K/AKT axis regulates a broad array of metabolic pathways, including glycolysis, the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP), oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), de novo lipogenesis, all of which contribute to tumor cell energy demands [ 4 ]. Aberrant activation of this pathway has been implicated in various aspects of cancer biology, such as enhanced glucose uptake, increased glycolytic flux, and altered redox homeostasis. However, the mechanisms by which PI3K/AKT influences key metabolic enzymes remain incompletely understood, particularly with respect to its direct regulation of glycolytic enzymes and the emerging non-canonical functions of these enzymes in tumor.

### The composition and activation mechanisms of the PI3K/AKT pathway
The PI3K/AKT axis is a central signaling pathway critically involved in regulating cell growth, survival, and metabolism. PI3K, a lipid kinase typically comprising a p110 catalytic subunit and p85/p55 regulatory subunits, is frequently dysregulated in human diseases, especially in cancer [ 3 ]. Based on structure and substrate specificity, PI3K can be categorized into three classes. Class I PI3Ks, the primary transducers of extracellular signals, are the most studied [ 3 ]. Activation of this pathway is triggered by various signals, including growth factors (e.g., EGF, IGF), cytokines (e.g., IL-6), hormones, and oncogene activation (e.g., RAS, MYC ) ( Fig. 1 ) [ 4 ]. These ligands bind to cell-surface receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs), such as EGFR, IGF-1R, or cytokine receptors, to initiate downstream signaling cascades. Upon activation, PI3K converts phosphatidylinositol (4,5)-bisphosphate (PIP2) to phosphatidylinositol (3,4,5)-trisphosphate (PIP3). PIP3 recruits AKT to the plasma membrane, where it is partially activated by phosphorylation at Thr308 by phosphoinositide-dependent kinase 1 (PDK1) and fully activated at Ser473 by mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 2 (mTORC2) [ 3 ]. This signaling cascade is negatively regulated by the tumor suppressor PTEN, which dephosphorylates PIP3 back to PIP2. In addition to PTEN-mediated repression, AKT activity is tightly controlled by serine/threonine phosphatase 2A (PP2A). The PP2A regulatory subunit PR130 (encoded by PPP2R3A ) is essential for assembling functional holoenzymes that restrain AKT signaling [ 5 , 6 ]. PP2A directly dephosphorylates AKT at Thr308 and Ser473, thereby suppressing downstream signaling [ 7 ]. Loss of PR130 disrupts PP2A-AKT binding and sustains AKT hyperactivation [ 5 , 6 ]. In hepatocellular carcinoma, aldolase B stabilizes the PP2A-AKT complex to further promote AKT dephosphorylation, underscoring PR130 as a key negative regulator of oncogenic AKT signaling [ 7 ]. AMPK, activated under energy shortage and suppressed in its surfeit, inversely regulates glycolysis in accordance with cellular metabolic status. When nutrients are abundant, AMPK attenuates aerobic glycolysis to restrain unnecessary anabolic processes. Conversely, under metabolic stress—particularly glucose scarcity—AMPK shifts its function to promote glycolysis, thereby sustaining ATP production and ensuring short-term cell viability. Activation of the PI3K/AKT axis typically suppresses AMPK activity through multiple mechanisms, including phosphorylating inhibitory sites of AMPK or downregulating upstream kinases of AMPK like LKB1. This inhibition relieves AMPK-mediated suppression of mTORC1 and aerobic glycolysis, allowing tumor cells to maintain a high level of anabolism and support their rapid proliferation and energy demands [ 44 , 45 ]. Consistent with this, studies have found that the deletion of PRKAA1/2 (AMPKα-encoding gene) can lead to an increase in the mRNA expression of ALDOA , LDHA and PDK1 , which all indicate that AMPK negatively regulates the glycolysis process of tumor cells and inhibits tumor growth [ 46 ]. Notably, AMPK can exert feedback regulatio

### Targeted therapeutic strategies for PI3K/AKT-mediated metabolic reprogramming
Metabolic reprogramming is a well-recognized adaptive hallmark of cancer cells, with aberrant glycolysis standing out as one of the most extensively characterized and therapeutically exploitable alterations. Targeting glycolytic enzymes and integrating these agents with other pathway-specific inhibitors or immunotherapies have emerged as promising strategies to overcome tumor cell survival advantages and drug resistance.

### Therapeutic targeting of metabolic enzymes in the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway
Aberrant glycolytic metabolism, a hallmark of cancer, offers a fertile ground for therapeutic intervention. By targeting key enzymes that drive this metabolic reprogramming, it is possible to disrupt the energy supply and biosynthetic pathways essential for cancer growth and survival. ### Conclusions and prospects
In conclusion, the PI3K/AKT axis plays a central role in cancer metabolic reprogramming. By precisely regulating key glycolytic metabolic enzymes (e.g., hexokinase, pyruvate kinase, phosphofructokinase, aldolase, lactate dehydrogenase) and related signaling molecules, it profoundly influences the metabolic phenotype of cancer cells. Rate-limiting glycolytic enzymes are subject to direct and indirect modulation by the PI3K/AKT signaling axis. Through alterations in their catalytic activity and expression levels, these enzymes collectively drive hallmark metabolic features of cancer cells, such as the Warburg effect. Rather than acting as a simple switch, this signaling axis executes precise control by modulating the subcellular distribution of key enzymes—such as the mitochondrial association of HK2 and the nuclear translocation of PKM2. These modifications not only drive the classical Warburg effect but also trigger "moonlighting" functions of metabolic enzymes that promote cell survival and immune evasion. Furthermore, the crosstalk between PI3K/AKT and the AMPK sensor ensures that glucose flux is strategically shunted into the PPP and biosynthetic processes to maintain redox balance. Through remodeling glycolytic metabolism, the PI3K/AKT axis further provides cancer cells with sufficient energy supply, essential biosynthetic raw materials, and effective antioxidant protection. Beyond solid tumors, we also emphasize the necessity of considering the unique features of hematological malignancies. Collectively, these molecular mechanism insights demonstrate that targeting the PI3K/AKT-centered metabolic regulatory network is a promising and sophisticated strategy for future precision cancer therapy.

### Highlights
• Focuses on the PI3K/AKT axis– its core link to cancer metabolic reprogramming (especially the Warburg Effect) and interaction with key glucose metabolic enzymes (HK, LDHA, etc.), as well as their impacts.
• 2. Introduces the non-canonical/moonlighting functions of these glucose metabolic enzymes.
• 3. Provides theoretical basis and potential targets for tumor metabolism research and targeted therapy, along with current research challenges and future directions.

### Introduction
Metabolic reprogramming is a hallmark of cancer, underpinning the rapid proliferation and survival of cancer cells. A cornerstone of this phenomenon is the Warburg effect, where tumor cells predominantly rely on glycolysis for energy even in the presence of oxygen, supports rapid cell proliferation by generating ATP and providing intermediates for biosynthesis processes, such as protein, lipid and nucleotide synthesis [ 1 , 2 ]. This reprogrammed glycolytic phenotype is orchestrated by multiple oncogenic pathways, among which the PI3K/AKT axis represents one of the most potent and commonly activated drivers. Abnormal activation of the PI3K/AKT axis is common in cancer and plays a crucial role in this metabolic shift [ 3 ].
The PI3K/AKT axis regulates a broad array of metabolic pathways, including glycolysis, the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP), oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), de novo lipogenesis, all of which contribute to tumor cell energy demands [ 4 ]. Aberrant activation of this pathway has been implicated in various aspects of cancer biology, such as enhanced glucose uptake, increased glycolytic flux, and altered redox homeostasis. However, the mechanisms by which PI3K/AKT influences key metabolic enzymes remain incompletely understood, particularly with respect to its direct regulation of glycolytic enzymes and the emerging non-canonical functions of these enzymes in tumor.

### The composition and activation mechanisms of the PI3K/AKT pathway
The PI3K/AKT axis is a central signaling pathway critically involved in regulating cell growth, survival, and metabolism. PI3K, a lipid kinase typically comprising a p110 catalytic subunit and p85/p55 regulatory subunits, is frequently dysregulated in human diseases, especially in cancer [ 3 ]. Based on structure and substrate specificity, PI3K can be categorized into three classes. Class I PI3Ks, the primary transducers of extracellular signals, are the most studied [ 3 ]. Activation of this pathway is triggered by various signals, including growth factors (e.g., EGF, IGF), cytokines (e.g., IL-6), hormones, and oncogene activation (e.g., RAS, MYC ) ( Fig. 1 ) [ 4 ]. These ligands bind to cell-surface receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs), such as EGFR, IGF-1R, or cytokine receptors, to initiate downstream signaling cascades. Upon activation, PI3K converts phosphatidylinositol (4,5)-bisphosphate (PIP2) to phosphatidylinositol (3,4,5)-trisphosphate (PIP3). PIP3 recruits AKT to the plasma membrane, where it is partially activated by phosphorylation at Thr308 by phosphoinositide-dependent kinase 1 (PDK1) and fully activated at Ser473 by mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 2 (mTORC2) [ 3 ]. This signaling cascade is negatively regulated by the tumor suppressor PTEN, which dephosphorylates PIP3 back to PIP2. In addition to PTEN-mediated repression, AKT activity is tightly controlled by serine/threonine phosphatase 2A (PP2A). The PP2A regulatory subunit PR130 (encoded by PPP2R3A ) is essential for assembling functional holoenzymes that restrain AKT signaling [ 5 , 6 ]. PP2A directly dephosphorylates AKT at Thr308 and Ser473, thereby suppressing downstream signaling [ 7 ]. Loss of PR130 disrupts PP2A-AKT binding and sustains AKT hyperactivation [ 5 , 6 ]. In hepatocellular carcinoma, aldolase B stabilizes the PP2A-AKT complex to further promote AKT dephosphorylation, underscoring PR130 as a key negative regulator of oncogenic AKT signaling [ 7 ]. ### PI3K/AKT-mediated direct regulation of glycolytic enzymes: metabolic catalysis and emerging non-metabolic roles
In cancer cells, the reprogramming of glucose metabolism is executed by the precise modulation of key glycolytic enzymes. The PI3K/AKT axis sits at the apex of this regulatory network, controlling both the activity and expression of these enzymes to drive the Warburg effect. We illustrate the main steps of glucose metabolism and the regulation of the PI3K/AKT pathway ( Fig. 2 ), and also elaborate on the non-canonical functions of these glycolytic enzymes.
Schematic Illustration of PI3K/AKT-driven Metabolic Reprogramming in Tumor Cells. Activated PI3K/AKT signaling rewires core glucose metabolism by upregulating glycolytic enzymes (HK2, PFK, PKM2, LDHA) to trigger the Warburg effect. Mechanistically, PI3K/AKT-activated PDK1 (3-phosphoinositide-dependent protein kinase 1) suppresses PDH (pyruvate dehydrogenase) activity, restricting pyruvate flux into the TCA (tricarboxylic acid) cycle and subsequent mitochondrial OXPHOS. PI3K/AKT simultaneously promotes PPP-derived NADPH production coupled with GSH (glutathione) to maintain redox homeostasis, and drives de novo lipogenesis via ACLY- and FASN-mediated cascades to fuel cell proliferation, with metabolic crosstalk between de novo lipogenesis and the TCA cycle. ROS (reactive oxygen species) generated by dysfunctional mitochondrial ETC (electron transport chain) I-V reciprocally reactivate upstream PI3K/AKT signaling, forming a positive feedback loop. Small molecule inhibitors targeting PI3K/AKT, key glycolytic enzymes, and OXPHOS are indicated in the diagram. Hexokinase: PI3K/AKT regulation and moonlighting functions
HK is the first rate-limiting enzyme in glycolysis, catalyzing the phosphorylation of glucose to produce glucose-6-phosphate, thereby trapping glucose inside the cell and initiating glycolytic flux. Accumulating evidence confirms a direct correlation between tumor cell growth rate and HK activity [ 18 ]. Among the four HK isoforms (HK1 to HK4), HK2 is of particular importance in cancer. ### Other signaling pathways interacting with the PI3K/AKT pathway
The PI3K/AKT signaling axis acts as a significant regulator of energy metabolism and redox homeostasis, exerting dual effects on the AMPK energy-sensing pathway and multiple glycolysis-associated metabolic pathways. By engaging in reciprocal regulatory crosstalk with AMPK, PI3K/AKT fine-tunes the balance between anabolic and catabolic processes to meet the metabolic demands of cells. Meanwhile, PI3K/AKT modulates PPP, OXPHOS, and de novo lipogenesis—key branches interconnected with glycolysis—to orchestrate metabolic networks that support cell proliferation, survival, and malignant progression.
Crosstalk with AMPK: reciprocal regulation between PI3K/AKT axis and energy sensor
AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) serves as a cellular energy receptor that is activated upon elevation of the AMP/ATP ratio. AMPK, activated under energy shortage and suppressed in its surfeit, inversely regulates glycolysis in accordance with cellular metabolic status. When nutrients are abundant, AMPK attenuates aerobic glycolysis to restrain unnecessary anabolic processes. Conversely, under metabolic stress—particularly glucose scarcity—AMPK shifts its function to promote glycolysis, thereby sustaining ATP production and ensuring short-term cell viability. Activation of the PI3K/AKT axis typically suppresses AMPK activity through multiple mechanisms, including phosphorylating inhibitory sites of AMPK or downregulating upstream kinases of AMPK like LKB1. This inhibition relieves AMPK-mediated suppression of mTORC1 and aerobic glycolysis, allowing tumor cells to maintain a high level of anabolism and support their rapid proliferation and energy demands [ 44 , 45 ]. Consistent with this, studies have found that the deletion of PRKAA1/2 (AMPKα-encoding gene) can lead to an increase in the mRNA expression of ALDOA , LDHA and PDK1 , which all indicate that AMPK negatively regulates the glycolysis process of tumor cells and inhibits tumor growth [ 46 ]. ### Conclusions and prospects
In conclusion, the PI3K/AKT axis plays a central role in cancer metabolic reprogramming. By precisely regulating key glycolytic metabolic enzymes (e.g., hexokinase, pyruvate kinase, phosphofructokinase, aldolase, lactate dehydrogenase) and related signaling molecules, it profoundly influences the metabolic phenotype of cancer cells. Rate-limiting glycolytic enzymes are subject to direct and indirect modulation by the PI3K/AKT signaling axis. Through alterations in their catalytic activity and expression levels, these enzymes collectively drive hallmark metabolic features of cancer cells, such as the Warburg effect. Rather than acting as a simple switch, this signaling axis executes precise control by modulating the subcellular distribution of key enzymes—such as the mitochondrial association of HK2 and the nuclear translocation of PKM2. These modifications not only drive the classical Warburg effect but also trigger "moonlighting" functions of metabolic enzymes that promote cell survival and immune evasion. Furthermore, the crosstalk between PI3K/AKT and the AMPK sensor ensures that glucose flux is strategically shunted into the PPP and biosynthetic processes to maintain redox balance. Through remodeling glycolytic metabolism, the PI3K/AKT axis further provides cancer cells with sufficient energy supply, essential biosynthetic raw materials, and effective antioxidant protection. Beyond solid tumors, we also emphasize the necessity of considering the unique features of hematological malignancies. Collectively, these molecular mechanism insights demonstrate that targeting the PI3K/AKT-centered metabolic regulatory network is a promising and sophisticated strategy for future precision cancer therapy.

### Highlights
• Focuses on the PI3K/AKT axis– its core link to cancer metabolic reprogramming (especially the Warburg Effect) and interaction with key glucose metabolic enzymes (HK, LDHA, etc.), as well as their impacts.
• 2. Introduces the non-canonical/moonlighting functions of these glucose metabolic enzymes.
• 3. Provides theoretical basis and potential targets for tumor metabolism research and targeted therapy, along with current research challenges and future directions.

### Introduction
Metabolic reprogramming is a hallmark of cancer, underpinning the rapid proliferation and survival of cancer cells. A cornerstone of this phenomenon is the Warburg effect, where tumor cells predominantly rely on glycolysis for energy even in the presence of oxygen, supports rapid cell proliferation by generating ATP and providing intermediates for biosynthesis processes, such as protein, lipid and nucleotide synthesis [ 1 , 2 ]. This reprogrammed glycolytic phenotype is orchestrated by multiple oncogenic pathways, among which the PI3K/AKT axis represents one of the most potent and commonly activated drivers. Abnormal activation of the PI3K/AKT axis is common in cancer and plays a crucial role in this metabolic shift [ 3 ].
The PI3K/AKT axis regulates a broad array of metabolic pathways, including glycolysis, the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP), oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), de novo lipogenesis, all of which contribute to tumor cell energy demands [ 4 ]. Aberrant activation of this pathway has been implicated in various aspects of cancer biology, such as enhanced glucose uptake, increased glycolytic flux, and altered redox homeostasis. However, the mechanisms by which PI3K/AKT influences key metabolic enzymes remain incompletely understood, particularly with respect to its direct regulation of glycolytic enzymes and the emerging non-canonical functions of these enzymes in tumor.

### The composition and activation mechanisms of the PI3K/AKT pathway
The PI3K/AKT axis is a central signaling pathway critically involved in regulating cell growth, survival, and metabolism. PI3K, a lipid kinase typically comprising a p110 catalytic subunit and p85/p55 regulatory subunits, is frequently dysregulated in human diseases, especially in cancer [ 3 ]. Based on structure and substrate specificity, PI3K can be categorized into three classes. Class I PI3Ks, the primary transducers of extracellular signals, are the most studied [ 3 ]. Activation of this pathway is triggered by various signals, including growth factors (e.g., EGF, IGF), cytokines (e.g., IL-6), hormones, and oncogene activation (e.g., RAS, MYC ) ( Fig. 1 ) [ 4 ]. These ligands bind to cell-surface receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs), such as EGFR, IGF-1R, or cytokine receptors, to initiate downstream signaling cascades. Upon activation, PI3K converts phosphatidylinositol (4,5)-bisphosphate (PIP2) to phosphatidylinositol (3,4,5)-trisphosphate (PIP3). PIP3 recruits AKT to the plasma membrane, where it is partially activated by phosphorylation at Thr308 by phosphoinositide-dependent kinase 1 (PDK1) and fully activated at Ser473 by mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 2 (mTORC2) [ 3 ]. This signaling cascade is negatively regulated by the tumor suppressor PTEN, which dephosphorylates PIP3 back to PIP2. In addition to PTEN-mediated repression, AKT activity is tightly controlled by serine/threonine phosphatase 2A (PP2A). The PP2A regulatory subunit PR130 (encoded by PPP2R3A ) is essential for assembling functional holoenzymes that restrain AKT signaling [ 5 , 6 ]. PP2A directly dephosphorylates AKT at Thr308 and Ser473, thereby suppressing downstream signaling [ 7 ]. Loss of PR130 disrupts PP2A-AKT binding and sustains AKT hyperactivation [ 5 , 6 ]. In hepatocellular carcinoma, aldolase B stabilizes the PP2A-AKT complex to further promote AKT dephosphorylation, underscoring PR130 as a key negative regulator of oncogenic AKT signaling [ 7 ]. ### PI3K/AKT-mediated direct regulation of glycolytic enzymes: metabolic catalysis and emerging non-metabolic roles
In cancer cells, the reprogramming of glucose metabolism is executed by the precise modulation of key glycolytic enzymes. The PI3K/AKT axis sits at the apex of this regulatory network, controlling both the activity and expression of these enzymes to drive the Warburg effect. We illustrate the main steps of glucose metabolism and the regulation of the PI3K/AKT pathway ( Fig. 2 ), and also elaborate on the non-canonical functions of these glycolytic enzymes.
Schematic Illustration of PI3K/AKT-driven Metabolic Reprogramming in Tumor Cells. Activated PI3K/AKT signaling rewires core glucose metabolism by upregulating glycolytic enzymes (HK2, PFK, PKM2, LDHA) to trigger the Warburg effect. Mechanistically, PI3K/AKT-activated PDK1 (3-phosphoinositide-dependent protein kinase 1) suppresses PDH (pyruvate dehydrogenase) activity, restricting pyruvate flux into the TCA (tricarboxylic acid) cycle and subsequent mitochondrial OXPHOS. PI3K/AKT simultaneously promotes PPP-derived NADPH production coupled with GSH (glutathione) to maintain redox homeostasis, and drives de novo lipogenesis via ACLY- and FASN-mediated cascades to fuel cell proliferation, with metabolic crosstalk between de novo lipogenesis and the TCA cycle. ROS (reactive oxygen species) generated by dysfunctional mitochondrial ETC (electron transport chain) I-V reciprocally reactivate upstream PI3K/AKT signaling, forming a positive feedback loop. Small molecule inhibitors targeting PI3K/AKT, key glycolytic enzymes, and OXPHOS are indicated in the diagram. Hexokinase: PI3K/AKT regulation and moonlighting functions
HK is the first rate-limiting enzyme in glycolysis, catalyzing the phosphorylation of glucose to produce glucose-6-phosphate, thereby trapping glucose inside the cell and initiating glycolytic flux. Accumulating evidence confirms a direct correlation between tumor cell growth rate and HK activity [ 18 ]. Among the four HK isoforms (HK1 to HK4), HK2 is of particular importance in cancer. ### Other signaling pathways interacting with the PI3K/AKT pathway
The PI3K/AKT signaling axis acts as a significant regulator of energy metabolism and redox homeostasis, exerting dual effects on the AMPK energy-sensing pathway and multiple glycolysis-associated metabolic pathways. By engaging in reciprocal regulatory crosstalk with AMPK, PI3K/AKT fine-tunes the balance between anabolic and catabolic processes to meet the metabolic demands of cells. Meanwhile, PI3K/AKT modulates PPP, OXPHOS, and de novo lipogenesis—key branches interconnected with glycolysis—to orchestrate metabolic networks that support cell proliferation, survival, and malignant progression.
Crosstalk with AMPK: reciprocal regulation between PI3K/AKT axis and energy sensor
AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) serves as a cellular energy receptor that is activated upon elevation of the AMP/ATP ratio. AMPK, activated under energy shortage and suppressed in its surfeit, inversely regulates glycolysis in accordance with cellular metabolic status. When nutrients are abundant, AMPK attenuates aerobic glycolysis to restrain unnecessary anabolic processes. Conversely, under metabolic stress—particularly glucose scarcity—AMPK shifts its function to promote glycolysis, thereby sustaining ATP production and ensuring short-term cell viability. Activation of the PI3K/AKT axis typically suppresses AMPK activity through multiple mechanisms, including phosphorylating inhibitory sites of AMPK or downregulating upstream kinases of AMPK like LKB1. This inhibition relieves AMPK-mediated suppression of mTORC1 and aerobic glycolysis, allowing tumor cells to maintain a high level of anabolism and support their rapid proliferation and energy demands [ 44 , 45 ]. Consistent with this, studies have found that the deletion of PRKAA1/2 (AMPKα-encoding gene) can lead to an increase in the mRNA expression of ALDOA , LDHA and PDK1 , which all indicate that AMPK negatively regulates the glycolysis process of tumor cells and inhibits tumor growth [ 46 ]. ### Targeted therapeutic strategies for PI3K/AKT-mediated metabolic reprogramming
Metabolic reprogramming is a well-recognized adaptive hallmark of cancer cells, with aberrant glycolysis standing out as one of the most extensively characterized and therapeutically exploitable alterations. Targeting glycolytic enzymes and integrating these agents with other pathway-specific inhibitors or immunotherapies have emerged as promising strategies to overcome tumor cell survival advantages and drug resistance.

### Therapeutic targeting of metabolic enzymes in the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway
Aberrant glycolytic metabolism, a hallmark of cancer, offers a fertile ground for therapeutic intervention. By targeting key enzymes that drive this metabolic reprogramming, it is possible to disrupt the energy supply and biosynthetic pathways essential for cancer growth and survival. ### Conclusions and prospects
In conclusion, the PI3K/AKT axis plays a central role in cancer metabolic reprogramming. By precisely regulating key glycolytic metabolic enzymes (e.g., hexokinase, pyruvate kinase, phosphofructokinase, aldolase, lactate dehydrogenase) and related signaling molecules, it profoundly influences the metabolic phenotype of cancer cells. Rate-limiting glycolytic enzymes are subject to direct and indirect modulation by the PI3K/AKT signaling axis. Through alterations in their catalytic activity and expression levels, these enzymes collectively drive hallmark metabolic features of cancer cells, such as the Warburg effect. Rather than acting as a simple switch, this signaling axis executes precise control by modulating the subcellular distribution of key enzymes—such as the mitochondrial association of HK2 and the nuclear translocation of PKM2. These modifications not only drive the classical Warburg effect but also trigger "moonlighting" functions of metabolic enzymes that promote cell survival and immune evasion. Furthermore, the crosstalk between PI3K/AKT and the AMPK sensor ensures that glucose flux is strategically shunted into the PPP and biosynthetic processes to maintain redox balance. Through remodeling glycolytic metabolism, the PI3K/AKT axis further provides cancer cells with sufficient energy supply, essential biosynthetic raw materials, and effective antioxidant protection. Beyond solid tumors, we also emphasize the necessity of considering the unique features of hematological malignancies. Collectively, these molecular mechanism insights demonstrate that targeting the PI3K/AKT-centered metabolic regulatory network is a promising and sophisticated strategy for future precision cancer therapy.

### Highlights
• Focuses on the PI3K/AKT axis– its core link to cancer metabolic reprogramming (especially the Warburg Effect) and interaction with key glucose metabolic enzymes (HK, LDHA, etc.), as well as their impacts.
• 2. Introduces the non-canonical/moonlighting functions of these glucose metabolic enzymes.
• 3. Provides theoretical basis and potential targets for tumor metabolism research and targeted therapy, along with current research challenges and future directions.

### Introduction
Metabolic reprogramming is a hallmark of cancer, underpinning the rapid proliferation and survival of cancer cells. A cornerstone of this phenomenon is the Warburg effect, where tumor cells predominantly rely on glycolysis for energy even in the presence of oxygen, supports rapid cell proliferation by generating ATP and providing intermediates for biosynthesis processes, such as protein, lipid and nucleotide synthesis [ 1 , 2 ]. This reprogrammed glycolytic phenotype is orchestrated by multiple oncogenic pathways, among which the PI3K/AKT axis represents one of the most potent and commonly activated drivers. Abnormal activation of the PI3K/AKT axis is common in cancer and plays a crucial role in this metabolic shift [ 3 ].
The PI3K/AKT axis regulates a broad array of metabolic pathways, including glycolysis, the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP), oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), de novo lipogenesis, all of which contribute to tumor cell energy demands [ 4 ]. Aberrant activation of this pathway has been implicated in various aspects of cancer biology, such as enhanced glucose uptake, increased glycolytic flux, and altered redox homeostasis. However, the mechanisms by which PI3K/AKT influences key metabolic enzymes remain incompletely understood, particularly with respect to its direct regulation of glycolytic enzymes and the emerging non-canonical functions of these enzymes in tumor.

### The composition and activation mechanisms of the PI3K/AKT pathway
The PI3K/AKT axis is a central signaling pathway critically involved in regulating cell growth, survival, and metabolism. PI3K, a lipid kinase typically comprising a p110 catalytic subunit and p85/p55 regulatory subunits, is frequently dysregulated in human diseases, especially in cancer [ 3 ]. Based on structure and substrate specificity, PI3K can be categorized into three classes. Class I PI3Ks, the primary transducers of extracellular signals, are the most studied [ 3 ]. Activation of this pathway is triggered by various signals, including growth factors (e.g., EGF, IGF), cytokines (e.g., IL-6), hormones, and oncogene activation (e.g., RAS, MYC ) ( Fig. 1 ) [ 4 ]. These ligands bind to cell-surface receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs), such as EGFR, IGF-1R, or cytokine receptors, to initiate downstream signaling cascades. Upon activation, PI3K converts phosphatidylinositol (4,5)-bisphosphate (PIP2) to phosphatidylinositol (3,4,5)-trisphosphate (PIP3). PIP3 recruits AKT to the plasma membrane, where it is partially activated by phosphorylation at Thr308 by phosphoinositide-dependent kinase 1 (PDK1) and fully activated at Ser473 by mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 2 (mTORC2) [ 3 ]. This signaling cascade is negatively regulated by the tumor suppressor PTEN, which dephosphorylates PIP3 back to PIP2. In addition to PTEN-mediated repression, AKT activity is tightly controlled by serine/threonine phosphatase 2A (PP2A). The PP2A regulatory subunit PR130 (encoded by PPP2R3A ) is essential for assembling functional holoenzymes that restrain AKT signaling [ 5 , 6 ]. PP2A directly dephosphorylates AKT at Thr308 and Ser473, thereby suppressing downstream signaling [ 7 ]. Loss of PR130 disrupts PP2A-AKT binding and sustains AKT hyperactivation [ 5 , 6 ]. In hepatocellular carcinoma, aldolase B stabilizes the PP2A-AKT complex to further promote AKT dephosphorylation, underscoring PR130 as a key negative regulator of oncogenic AKT signaling [ 7 ]. ### PI3K/AKT-mediated direct regulation of glycolytic enzymes: metabolic catalysis and emerging non-metabolic roles
In cancer cells, the reprogramming of glucose metabolism is executed by the precise modulation of key glycolytic enzymes. The PI3K/AKT axis sits at the apex of this regulatory network, controlling both the activity and expression of these enzymes to drive the Warburg effect. We illustrate the main steps of glucose metabolism and the regulation of the PI3K/AKT pathway ( Fig. 2 ), and also elaborate on the non-canonical functions of these glycolytic enzymes.
Schematic Illustration of PI3K/AKT-driven Metabolic Reprogramming in Tumor Cells. Activated PI3K/AKT signaling rewires core glucose metabolism by upregulating glycolytic enzymes (HK2, PFK, PKM2, LDHA) to trigger the Warburg effect. Mechanistically, PI3K/AKT-activated PDK1 (3-phosphoinositide-dependent protein kinase 1) suppresses PDH (pyruvate dehydrogenase) activity, restricting pyruvate flux into the TCA (tricarboxylic acid) cycle and subsequent mitochondrial OXPHOS. PI3K/AKT simultaneously promotes PPP-derived NADPH production coupled with GSH (glutathione) to maintain redox homeostasis, and drives de novo lipogenesis via ACLY- and FASN-mediated cascades to fuel cell proliferation, with metabolic crosstalk between de novo lipogenesis and the TCA cycle. ROS (reactive oxygen species) generated by dysfunctional mitochondrial ETC (electron transport chain) I-V reciprocally reactivate upstream PI3K/AKT signaling, forming a positive feedback loop. Small molecule inhibitors targeting PI3K/AKT, key glycolytic enzymes, and OXPHOS are indicated in the diagram. Hexokinase: PI3K/AKT regulation and moonlighting functions
HK is the first rate-limiting enzyme in glycolysis, catalyzing the phosphorylation of glucose to produce glucose-6-phosphate, thereby trapping glucose inside the cell and initiating glycolytic flux. Accumulating evidence confirms a direct correlation between tumor cell growth rate and HK activity [ 18 ]. Among the four HK isoforms (HK1 to HK4), HK2 is of particular importance in cancer.
